research_concepts: unit-level effectiveness (>=70% of units with lift>0, median lift>2pp)
methodological_questions: definition of PNR failure (event/threshold, independence from outcome)
definition of pull-up counter (temporal sequencing, play-type labeling)
unit of analysis (team, lineup, or player)
baseline for lift (expected PPP given situation, avoiding RTM)
sample size per unit for failed-PNR-then-pull-up sequences
estimation and inference on the proportion of units with lift>0 and median lift
confounding by defensive adjustment after PNR failure
measurement reliability of play-type labels (PNR, PULL_UP)
regression to the mean from selecting on low-outcome possessions

historical_evidence.finding: Within-game adaptation inferred from early-third PPP and subsequent shift toward counter play types produced apparent lifts (+0.058 PPP), but the no-signal baseline was highest and the effect was a mean-reversion artifact; within-scheme controls dissolved the lift.

A1 adapter PPP lift (+0.0667 for adapters vs +0.1260 for no_signal) was not a real coverage response; wrong-way teams did not do worse, confidence did not increase gap, and carryover was absent—all pointing to construction/labeling artifact.

On-ball defensive scheme labels (DROP/ICE/SWITCH) could be assigned at confident rates of only 14.9% and 3.3% for DET and ORL respectively; switches_on was never populated, making scheme-based conditioning unreliable.

Raw turnover-force channel lifts shrunk by ~50% or more when opponent re-route or follow-the-ball counter was accounted for; net lifts were model-implied, not observed directly, and surrogate counters often had n<10.

Playoff defenses allowed much higher PULL_UP PPP (+0.341) than regular season, while PULL_UP share dropped 7.6 pp and PNR share jumped 12.1 pp, though tagging differences could explain part of the shift.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Within-game adaptation inference using early-third PPP to infer opponent scheme and later shift toward counter play types
failed_approaches.why: Selection on early-third PPP extremes induced regression to the mean; no-signal baseline showed highest PPP, indicating the apparent lift was an artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Falsification tests for adapter PPP lift (asymmetry, confidence, carryover)
failed_approaches.why: Apparent adapter lift was an artifact of selection or labeling; adapter-minus-no-signal deltas were negative, and carryover test (Welch t = -1.003, p=0.842) failed to distinguish adapters.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Labeling on-ball defensive schemes (DROP/ICE/SWITCH) from matchup/PBP fields
failed_approaches.why: Confident label rates were far below usable thresholds (14.9% and 3.3%); switches_on never populated, making scheme-based inference impossible.

evidence_establishes: Prior attempts to measure within-game adaptation lift by selecting on early possession outcomes were artefactual due to regression to the mean.
Defensive scheme labeling from standard NBA data feeds is too sparse and unreliable to condition on coverage type.
Apparent lifts from turnover-forcing or counter strategies shrink substantially when opponent re-routing and counters are incorporated.
evidence_does_not_establish: No study directly tested the effect of switching to a pull-up after a failed PNR on league-wide unit-level effectiveness.
The reliability of play-type labels (PNR vs PULL_UP) in the derived possession records is not evaluated; prior failures were with defensive schemes, not offensive play types.
No evidence on whether a properly constructed baseline (e.g., pull-up PPP in similar situations without a prior PNR failure) would eliminate regression artefacts in this specific counter.
own_inferences: The question's definition of 'PNR fail' almost certainly relies on the outcome of the PNR possession (points, turnover), creating a strong regression-toward-the-mean bias, as demonstrated by SF13 and SF-APPA-001.
Even if a non-outcome definition of failure could be devised (e.g., a forced pass from a trap), the data lack reliable defensive event labels, making such a definition infeasible.

The unit of analysis is underspecified; likely units are teams, giving at most 30 units, which makes the 70% threshold (>=21 teams) sensitive to small-sample noise in each team's lift estimate and reduces power to detect a true median lift of 2pp.

The requirement that lift be a 'real league-wide counter' calls for a causal interpretation that cannot be supported without a design that controls for defensive adjustments and endogenous play selection—neither of which is possible with only observational possession records.

A viable test would need to define failure independently of outcome (defensive action, shot clock, location) and compare pull-up PPP after failure to pull-up PPP after non-failure PNRs, with within-unit randomization or at least season-level aggregation to avoid within-game selection bias; this is extremely demanding.
uncertainties: The exact accuracy of derived play-type labels (PNR, PULL_UP) in the possession graph is unknown; labeling errors could add noise or bias.
The available multi-season data may provide enough sequences per team to estimate unit-level lift with reasonable precision, but this is uncertain without exploratory analysis.

There may exist a subset of clear PNR failures (e.g., shot-clock violations, blocked shots) that are less affected by random outcome variance, but the resulting sample size per unit would likely be very small.

The hypothesis could be reinterpreted as a purely descriptive pattern (teams that use pull-ups after failed PNRs tend to have better outcomes than teams that do not), but the phrasing 'real league-wide counter' implies a causal claim that the data cannot sustain.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical records, I would have considered the question testable with a straightforward pre-post PPP comparison within units, albeit with power concerns. The retrieval showed that nearly identical adaptation studies (SF13, SF-APPA-001) produced artefactual results due to regression to the mean and selection bias, and that defensive scheme labels are too sparse to define failure independently. This strongly shifts the assessment toward do_not_proceed, as the same pitfalls are likely to afflict a 'PNR fail then PULL_UP' lift study unless very strong controls are applied.

blocking_constraints.text: Defining PNR failure by possession outcome (low points, turnover) selects on the lower tail of the distribution, causing subsequent possessions to regress to the mean regardless of play type.

Defensive adjustments after a failed PNR (e.g., switching coverage, dropping back) directly affect the success of a subsequent pull-up, making it impossible to isolate the causal effect of the counter strategy.

Within-unit sample sizes of failed-PNR-then-pull-up sequences are likely small, leading to imprecise lift estimates and low power to classify 70% of units as having lift>0 or to estimate median lift with acceptable error.
Play-type misclassification (PNR vs PULL_UP vs other) could bias lift estimates; the reliability of the possession graph's play-type labels has not been validated in the retrieved studies.

prior_work.summary: Prior studies on within-game adaptation and counter strategies (SF13, SF-APPA-001) found that apparent lifts are artefactual due to regression to the mean and selection bias. Defensive scheme labeling efforts (SF-APPS-058) failed because confident labels were too rare. Adversarial re-routing (SF-APPA-067) showed that first-stage lifts shrink substantially. These findings collectively indicate that any study defining 'failure' by outcome and measuring subsequent lift is at high risk of producing a spurious positive result.

risks.text: Likely the dominant risk: selecting PNR possessions that 'failed' (low points) will bias upward the apparent lift of any subsequent action because outcomes will naturally regress toward the mean.
Defensive strategy and game situation after a PNR failure may simultaneously cause both the use of a pull-up and its success rate, confounding the estimated counter effect.
The number of qualifying sequences per unit (team, lineup) may be too small to reliably estimate unit-level lift and to test the 70% and median criteria with useful power.
If play-type labels (PNR, PULL_UP) contain systematic or random errors, lift estimates will be biased or noisy; the data catalog's derived records have not been independently validated.
The base rate of pull-up usage immediately after a failed PNR may be low, making the counter strategy sparse and the lift estimates highly variable.

design.estimand: Causal effect of using a pull-up play type as the immediate offensive response to a failed pick-and-roll on the points scored in that pull-up possession, compared to the expected points from a pull-up in the same game situation absent the PNR failure, aggregated across units (teams) to test whether at least 70% of units show a positive effect and the median effect exceeds +0.02 PPP.
design.unit: NBA team-offense (30 units), with secondary analysis at the primary ball-handler level.
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff games from 2022-23 through 2025-26, restricted to possessions where a PNR is followed by the same offense's next possession (within same stint, no timeout or substitution) and that next possession is a pull-up; the control group would be pull-up possessions not immediately preceded by a failed PNR but matched on game context.
design.power: With 30 teams and approximately 10-30 qualifying sequences per team per season, the standard error of a team's lift estimate is likely >0.05 PPP, making it impossible to reliably classify 70% of teams as above zero or to estimate median lift with confidence intervals narrower than ±2pp. The study is underpowered for the stated thresholds.
design.controls: Must control for regression to the mean by using a baseline independent of the PNR outcome: e.g., season-average pull-up PPP in the same game state (score margin, quarter, possession start type). Must also adjust for defensive scheme changes by using a within-possession defensive event classifier, but such a classifier is not available reliably.
design.falsification: A placebo test: define a 'pseudo-failure' by randomly selecting PNR possessions with average outcomes and test whether pull-up PPP after these events shows the same lift. If the same pattern appears, the effect is due to selection or regression, not a genuine counter. Also, test whether the lift disappears when controlling for defensive transition metrics.
design.multiplicity: The primary claim involves two summary statistics (proportion >0 and median lift). No additional multiplicity correction needed, but any subgroup analyses (by player, coverage) would require adjustment.
design.decision_rule: Reject the hypothesis if the lower bound of a 95% bootstrap confidence interval for the proportion of units with lift>0 falls below 0.70 OR the upper bound of the 95% CI for median lift falls below 0.02 PPP, using a block-bootstrap by team to account for within-team dependence.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 postseason, using per-game play-by-play and derived play-type possession records as available on 2026-05-23.

args.query: If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, with lift>0 in >=70% of units and median lift>2pp.

reasoning_details.text:
We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions from the research question. The question: "If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp."

Interpretation: PNR stands for pick-and-roll. "If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter" - this seems to say: if pick-and-roll fails (i.e., when the defense successfully suppresses the PNR), then the offensive counter is to use a pull-up shot. The claim: this is a real league-wide counter. The test: it should show lift >0 in >=70% of units with median lift >2pp. "units" might be teams, or player types, or defensive schemes? "lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp" meaning across units (e.g., teams, or perhaps defensive matchups), at least 70% of them should have positive lift, and the median lift across units should be >2 percentage points. Lift likely means improvement in offensive efficiency (points per possession) when using pull-up shot after a failed PNR compared to some baseline. The phrase "defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)" suggests the research area is defensive suppression (defensive strategies that suppress certain offensive actions) and counter strategies (offensive adjustments). So the question proposes that when a defense successfully suppresses pick-and-roll, the offense counters with a pull-up shot, which should be effective league-wide. So we need to test if the pull-up is an effective counter to PNR failure.

Concepts: pick-and-roll (PNR) failure, pull-up shot as counter, lift (points per possession difference), league-wide effectiveness (generality across units), threshold: >0 lift in >=70% of units, median lift >2pp. Also, research area: defensive suppression and counter strategy.

Methodological questions: what constitutes a "unit"? (teams? player pairs? defensive matchups? seasons?). How to define "PNR fail"? When the offense runs a pick-and-roll possession and it results in a below-average points per possession? Or specifically when the defense's defensive matchup or scheme suppresses it? Might need definition of PNR failure from data: perhaps a PNR possession that ends without a score or with turnover, or low points. "PULL_UP" is a play type: pull-up jumper (shot off dribble). Need to define lift: compare points per possession (PPP) of possessions where a PNR failed and the next action is a pull-up vs. what baseline? Maybe baseline is all possessions after a failed PNR? Or average offensive PPP. Need to define counter: using pull-up after failed PNR.

Methodological questions: How to identify PNR possessions and whether they "failed"? How to detect that the offense responded with a pull-up? Does the possession sequence allow linking a failed PNR to a subsequent pull-up? The data includes play-by-play action type, sub-type, and derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points). So we could identify PNR possessions, their outcomes (points), and then see if after a failed PNR, the offense uses a pull-up shot. However, the question says "If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter" meaning if the PNR fails, the offense should then pull up. That implies the offense might have a sequence within a single possession? Typically a basketball possession might involve multiple actions: a pick-and-roll attempt, then if it fails (e.g., defender goes under, switches, or denies), the ball handler might pull up for a shot. This could happen within the same possession. The play-by-play data might record each action. So we need to define PNR failure as an action (like a pick and roll ball handler action) that doesn't yield points, and then the next action by the same team is a pull-up shot. That sequence would be a counter. So the lift of the pull-up after PNR failure would be the points scored on that pull-up compared to some expected points if they didn't pull up (maybe average points after a failed PNR when they do something else). Or it could be the change in efficiency from the failed action to the subsequent action.

Research concepts: "defensive suppression", "counter strategy", "best/avoid" framework, pick-and-roll failure, pull-up shot, lift (points per possession), league-wide generality, unit-level lift thresholds.

Methodological questions: What is an appropriate unit of analysis? The question mentions ">=70% of units" - likely teams, or maybe defensive matchup groups. Could be "team-season" units. Need to decide how to aggregate possessions into units. Also, what is the baseline for lift? Is it comparing PPP of possessions where after a PNR failure the team uses a pull-up vs. those where they don't? Or vs. league-average PPP? How to ensure independence and avoid lookahead bias? The definition of "PNR fail" might be determined before the pull-up is taken, so no lookahead if we only consider the action of PNR and then pull-up. But defining failure: if the PNR action didn't result in points, that's known at the time the pull-up is taken (the shot clock still running). So it's fine. Risks: sample size for specific units (some teams might have few such sequences), sparse data for some player/team combinations, measurement reliability of play-type classification (PNR and pull-up), possible confounding by game situation (score, time, defense quality), mechanical floor effects (some teams might always have low efficiency after failed PNR). Also, multiple testing if testing across many units (teams), but the claim is about 70% of units having lift>0, not individual significance. However, estimating median lift >2pp requires accurate estimation of each unit's lift, which has sampling error. The 70% threshold might be sensitive to estimation error. Also, the lift threshold 2pp per possession? "2pp" likely means 2 percentage points in points per possession (e.g., from 0.9 to 1.1 ppp, difference 0.2 ppp?). Actually "2pp" could mean 2 points per 100 possessions? In basketball analytics, "ppp" is points per possession, so "2pp" could be 0.02 ppp? Usually lift is expressed in points per 100 possessions, e.g., +2 points per 100 poss = +0.02 ppp. But "2pp" could be 2 points per game? Ambiguous. But methodological question: unit of measurement and sample size power.

Also: "league-wide counter" implies generalization across teams. So we need to test across all 30 teams, but 70% would be 21 teams. So sample of 30 might be enough, but per-team sample of sequences might be small. The median of team-level lifts (probably using Bayesian shrinkage or something) to avoid noisy extremes. But the statement "median lift>2pp" requires that median of estimated lifts >2pp. With small per-team samples, estimates are imprecise; the question doesn't specify how to handle uncertainty. Could use hierarchical modeling to get shrinkage estimates. That might be a methodological choice.

So research concepts: pick-and-roll failure, pull-up counter, lift, league-wide generalization, units. Methodological questions: definition of PNR failure and pull-up, unit of analysis, baseline for lift, sample size/power, estimation and uncertainty for median and threshold proportion, confounding, measurement reliability.
